<reason>Two strong, symmetrical cases: B (PRO) built a coherent "legitimacy hires, scopes, and revokes competence" frame and defended it well (alarm clock, mortal-vs-chronic errors, means/ends). A (CON) consistently landed the sharper turns: delegating institutions as democracy's own testimony that being right outranks being authorized, Venezuela reached through elected mandates, the Ulysses reversal, and above all the extracted concession that a fully authorized policy raising child mortality is still a bad decision — pressed decisively in the closing ("authorization is not what makes a public decision good"). A's meta-argument that every virtue B claims for legitimacy is an outcome, making results the master criterion, was never fully neutralized. B's clipped opening is a minor execution cost. A answered pressure questions directly, kept the burden comparison clean, and closed more memorably ("Consent tells you the room is yours. Competence tells you the roof will hold"). B's revocability frame remains live, keeping the margin thin.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The Q2 child-mortality exchange: A forced a yes/no on whether a democratically authorized, mortality-raising policy beat a correct unpopular expert; B conceded it was a bad decision but salvaged the systemic comparison ("democracy's errors are mortal; insulated errors are chronic"). A then converted the concession into the debate's decisive weighing point in Rebuttal 2 and the Closing, while B's "who demonstrates it?" defense blunted but did not erase it.</best_rebuttal>
